## Overview {#sec-overview}

This project focuses on data harmonization of multisite neuroimaging data using FreeSurfer-derived brain structural measurements. The goal is to investigate differences in brain measurements across sites and explore approaches to reduce site-related variability, improving the consistency and comparability of neuroimaging datasets. The project uses multisite data provided through the Penn NeuroBridge Lab.

[Final Project GitHub Repository](https://github.com/nlatifam/BMIN5030_Final_Project)

## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Neuroimaging is an important tool for studying brain structure and understanding neurological conditions. However, when MRI data are collected from multiple hospitals or research institutions, differences in scanners, imaging protocols, and acquisition methods can introduce unwanted variability into brain measurements. These differences can make it difficult to determine whether observed variations are caused by actual biological differences or technical factors. Data harmonization aims to reduce these site-related differences while preserving meaningful biological information. This project focuses on exploring data harmonization using multisite FreeSurfer-derived brain structural measurements to improve the consistency and comparability of neuroimaging data.

Addressing this challenge requires an interdisciplinary approach that combines neuroscience, biomedical informatics, and biostatistics. Through my work with Dr. Nishant Sinha at the Penn NeuroBridge Lab, I have been introduced to the computational challenges of analyzing neuroimaging data and the importance of ensuring data quality. Dr. Kristin Linn's research in biostatistics and neuroimaging provides another relevant perspective, particularly in developing statistical approaches to address variability across imaging sites. Neuroscience helps explain the biological significance of brain measurements, while biostatistics provides methods for identifying and adjusting for unwanted technical variation. Together, these fields demonstrate how interdisciplinary approaches can improve the reliability of neuroimaging research.

## Methods {#sec-methods}

This project uses a multisite neuroimaging dataset containing FreeSurfer-derived brain structural measurements, provided through the Penn NeuroBridge Lab. The initial analysis will focus on examining the structure and quality of the dataset, identifying missing values, and exploring potential differences in brain measurements across research sites. These exploratory analyses will help determine the extent of site-related variability and inform the selection of an appropriate data harmonization approach. Subsequent analyses will evaluate whether harmonization reduces unwanted site-related differences while preserving meaningful biological variation.

```{r}

library(readxl)

data <- read_excel("freesurferStats.xlsx")

dim(data)
names(data)
head(data)

# Examine the structure of the dataset
str(data)

# Check for missing values in each variable
colSums(is.na(data))

# Summarize participant demographics
summary(data)

# Examine control and patient groups
table(data$isControl, useNA = "ifany")

# Examine FreeSurfer versions
table(data$freeSurferVer, useNA = "ifany")

# Check for zero values in brain measurements
brain_cols <- grep("^(Left_|Right_)", names(data), value = TRUE)

colSums(data[brain_cols] == 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Identify participants with zero brain measurements
zero_rows <- rowSums(data[brain_cols] == 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Count participants with at least one zero
sum(zero_rows > 0)

# Examine affected participants
data[zero_rows > 0, c("record_id", "isControl", "freeSurferVer")]

# Count zero-valued brain regions for each affected participant
table(zero_rows[zero_rows > 0])
```

The dataset was imported into R using the `readxl` package. Initial exploratory analysis was performed to examine the dimensions, variable names, data types, and first six observations of the dataset. Missing values were assessed to identify potential data quality issues. Additional analyses examined the distribution of participant groups and FreeSurfer software versions to identify potential sources of variability. These steps provide an initial understanding of the dataset's structure and characteristics, helping inform subsequent data harmonization analyses.

Additional quality-control analysis identified five participants (0.8%) with zero-valued measurements across all 14 examined brain regions. Three were non-controls and two were controls. All five participants were processed using FreeSurfer version 7. These findings suggest potentially missing or unsuccessful brain segmentation measurements rather than true anatomical volumes. The five participants were flagged for potential exclusion from subsequent analyses, pending further investigation. Excluding these participants would leave 607 participants with nonzero measurements across the examined brain regions.

## Results {#sec-results}

Initial exploratory analysis identified 612 participants and 21 variables in the dataset. Of these participants, 305 (49.8%) were classified as controls and 307 (50.2%) as non-controls. All participants were processed using FreeSurfer version 7.

Missing-value analysis identified 498 missing values in `penn_record_id`, potentially reflecting the withholding of participant identifiers for privacy or de-identification purposes. No missing values were identified in the brain structural measurements.

These preliminary findings indicate that the structural brain measurements are complete. Further analysis will explore variability in brain measurements and determine whether sufficient information is available to investigate site-related differences and potential harmonization approaches.

Further quality-control analysis identified five zero values in each of the 14 brain-region measurements. Although these values were not recorded as missing (`NA`), they may represent unavailable measurements or segmentation-related issues. Additional investigation is needed to determine whether the zero values occur in the same participants and whether these observations should be excluded from subsequent analyses.
